utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning to everybody in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everyone in the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-83-T, The Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. May we have the appearances for today, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, to my learned colleagues from the Defence, General Delic, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis Matthias Neuner Laurie Sartorio, Kyle Wood and Aditya Menon, assisted by our case manager Djurdja Mirkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends. Good morning to everyone in and around the courtroom. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson for General Rasim Delic. Our assistants are Lana Deljkic, Lejla Gluhic, and Asja Zujo. We also have an intern Claire Bonnel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning. You may proceed, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'm just waiting for the computer screen. Thank you, Your Honours. I just want to give two small addendums relating to yesterday's part, because I couldn't bring the references for Your Honours' benefit. And I'm referring to the indicator that's the first question, I believe, question number 5, I tried -- or question number 8 I tried to address yesterday. The indicator was that ARBiH officers led ARBiH soldiers who were subordinated to the El Mujahedin Detachment; and in so far, I'm referring to page 76, lines 2 to 9 of yesterday's transcript. And I want -- I didn't know the exhibit. It is Exhibit 702, which is displayed here, Your Honours. It's from the 5th Mountain Battalion, an order; and I referred to Mr. Zilkic yesterday. You see in the first highlighted line: Pursuant to the verbal order issued by the commander of the 328th Brigade, that's Mr. Zilkic. Pursuant to that verbal order, Mr. Ahmet Sehic, who testified in front of Your Honours, issued this order: Number one, to select 30 men to carry the wounded. And in number four, Your Honours see that these men should be resubordinated to the El Mujahedin Detachment to carry the wounded. And number 3 is the point that the Prosecution was referring to yesterday. You can see what Mr. Sehic directs: The responsible officer in charge of this group shall be the 2nd Lieutenant Husein Fazlic, commander of the logistics platoon. So you have here, Mr. Sehic not only sending ordinary soldiers to carry the wounded, as the second echelon during combat activity involving the EMD, you have Mr. Sehic also sending one of his officers to go with the group, and obviously look and supervise the task. The second addendum, I talked about it only orally, fixing the start time for Proljece 2. This was part of the presentation on oral meetings before, during, and after joint combat. I didn't have the reference; and, yesterday, this is transcript page 80, lines 12 to 13. I have now have found PW-9's statement, consolidated Rule 92 ter statement; Exhibit 826, paragraph 212. What did Mr. PW-9 tell Your Honours? That the second operation started on the 22nd of July, and the exact time of that operation was agreed in the 35th Division command at the meeting. So there was a meeting prior to Proljece 2, the July operation; and in the 35th Division, the El Mujahedin Detachment showed up and the time, the exact time was agreed to. Moving on to the Defence pre-trial brief, paragraph 670, Your Honours. It is alleged by the Defence that the Prosecution has not presented any evidence that Delic knew that the EMD was taking part in Operation Farz. We say that Delic, indeed, knew that the EMD remained on the Vozuca battlefield after Operation Proljece 2. I have addressed the issue of Mr. Delic's knowledge, in our view at least, that he knew about the participation of the EMD before Proljece 2. And then during the ongoing Proljece 2, Your Honours have seen this yesterday, Exhibit 582, this document was received. It's a bulletin talking about wounded during the Operation Proljece 2, and it's mentioned that 15 members out of 18 killed, 15 out of 18 soldiers killed, were from the El Mujahedin Detachment, which corresponds to what the Prosecution believes is the first echelon. The El Mujahedin Detachment is an assault detachment, therefore its soldiers get primarily killed. We now submit, in relation to Farz, that after Operation Proljece 2 was over, Delic was never -- Commander Delic was never informed that the El Mujahedin Detachment had left the Ozren-Vozuca battlefield, nor that they had even the intention to leave the battlefield. Hence, the only logical conclusion is, if I as a commander order subsequent combat activity -- combat activities, who is going to take part? We have seen that the El Mujahedin Detachment soldiers were primarily killed in the first operation, Your Honours, in the Operation Proljece 2, in July. On the 2nd of August 1995, Your Honours have heard evidence that Mr. Delic visited the 35th Division headquarter in Zavidovici. Operation Proljece 2 was almost over, and he is visiting with Mr. Mahmuljin - that is Exhibit 460 - the 3rd Corps commander who definitely knows what his subordinate unit, meaning the El Mujahedin Detachment, is going to do or is not going to do. Mr. Delic was visiting the 35th Division which was, in the Prosecution's view, running Proljece 2 operation, commanding it in the chain of command of the ARBiH. On the 4th of August, 1995, there's a bulletin, Exhibit 740, which states that: After the loss of these positions of the 328th Mountain Brigade, rumours start in Zavidovici. And, again, it is misinformation according to the authors view of the bulletin, but there is a quarrel reported, probably a misinformation, between members of the EMD and the 7th Muslim Brigade over war booty. So, in our view, it is a clear indication that, obviously, the El Mujahedin Detachment is not passive in the zone of the 35th Division, but there are rumours about war booty, about whether there is combat activity or not involving the El Mujahedin Detachment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Neuner, was the EMD present at the meetings when General Delic visited the 35th Corps in August?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: This is a point which I left out consciously. As far as I can recall, Mr. Hasanagic testified that Mr. Aiman Awad was seen, I believe, entering the building while either he himself entered the building or Mr. Delic himself - I don't know myself - and that there was a meeting going on without him, as far as I understood, without Mr. Awad. Then Mr. Hasanagic's evidence was - I don't want to comment upon it - not clear, maybe, in the sense that he only saw him, Mr. Awad, going through the corridor. And there was a separate meeting; and as far as I have recollection now, he could not recall who was present at this meeting, including whether Mr. Awad was present at the meeting. So, therefore, I left this point out because I thought the Prosecution should not address this point. It is for Your Honours to decide what, if any, conclusion to draw from this. I want to address briefly the Vranduk reporting. Your Honours have heard that the propensity of the El Mujahedin Detachment to commit crimes and the reports about these crimes is contentious between the parties. And Mr. Vuckovic was asked generally about a Vranduk document, dating from 7 November 2007, roughly towards the end of the war. It's transcript page 5185, and the Exhibit is 662. And Mr. Vuckovic stated that the results of Vranduk were delivered to the head of the military security administration. He was asked and he stated yes. This is Mr. Jasarevic, Your Honours. Mr. Buljubasic, the chef de cabinet -- one of the chef de cabinet of Mr. Delic, in his 92 ter statement, paragraph 5, Exhibit 816, told Your Honours: Rasim Delic also met with General Hajrulahovic, Jusuf Jasarevic, and Fikret Mumovic. And he continues: Written communication between Rasim Delic and Jusuf Jasarevic was more frequent. Their meetings weren't more frequent than those which Rasim Delic had with the other chiefs of administration. The meetings with Mr. Jasarevic were based upon need. Again, Mr. Vuckovic told Your Honours, Exhibit 706, paragraph 33, the 92 ter statement, that Commander Delic was regularly informed through bulletins and, of course, at the meetings with the chief of the Security Administration, Jusuf Jasarevic. Can I ask that we move into private session Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to address the last topic. The Defence's denial that three ARBiH combat activities involved either the Mujahedin from Poljanice or the EMD, and I'm referring to Karaula, Vitez, and Teslic. Your Honours, we have address that issue already indirectly in paragraphs 53 and 54 of our final trial brief. Just some remarks. This is in relation to Karaula. Combat until November, from September until November 1992. If Your Honours look at the last line: According to Adilovic, they were not fighting with the ARBiH, referring here to the Mujahedin. We say the Mujahedin fought with and were under the subordination of the ARBiH in Karaula. Ali Hamad told Your Honour, the Presiding Judge, this very fact. Page 19 and 20 on the 7th of September 2007: Your Honour, the Presiding Judge, asked: Were there any other military forces in the area known as Karaula? And Mr. Hamad told or answered: Yes. There were members of the Croatian defence counsel at the time, we cooperated with the HVO; or rather, the Bosniaks cooperated with the HVO, and we, as foreign Mujahedin who were a part of the Bosnian units, had to respect that. And Your Honours clarified: What do you mean by Bosniaks? Mr. Hamad replies: I'm thinking precisely of members of the army of -- ARBiH. Mr. Hamad, being involved over a month in Karaula, feels as a part of the ARBiH. The second denial relates to Vitez. Combat occurring when the El Mujahedin Detachment is already formed. We say, in the OTP, the EMD indeed participated in combat in Vitez in September 1993, and the ARBiH knew about it. Why? Mr. Awad testified to Your Honours, page 59 and 60 on the 8th of February, 2008: "There was a meeting with unit commanders." It was related to combat operations, Your Honours. Vitez: "Wahiuddin was called to the meeting." Mr. Awad is asked: Who was also present? Mr. General Mehmed Alagic, he replies. Then he goes on: "There wasn't a lot of talk. Wahiuddin just presented the facts that people were on the ground and that these combat operations needed to be continued. As far as I understood, there had already been an attack and that it should be continued. First of all, we say that this is reporting, Your Honours. Wahiuddin, the then-military commander, is summoned by Mr. Alagic to a meeting. He is not only showing up; he is reporting. And then what comes out of that meeting, Mr. Awad continues: "We returned," referring to the El Mujahedin Detachment, "Wahiuddin and myself to Kruscica, where the El Mujahedin Detachment unit was stationed, and then they tried to carry out an attack against a position called Crveno Brdo, I think. But we had many wounded, high losses, and we couldn't reach that spot where the men were assigned to go. The operation was not successful, but Your Honours see. I want to deal with the last denial, and this is combat in OG North in 1994, paragraph 895 of the Defence pre-trial brief: The EMD's military emir, Muatez, refused to permit the EMD to participate in the action at Pisana Jelika and Visoka Glava. And the last words: The EMD carried the action independently when it thought it should do so, despite the 3rd Corps order for joint action with other units. Just to recap. Exhibit 837 tells Your Honours it is a 3rd Corps attack decision on the 20th of August, 1994. Number two is the El Mujahedin Detachment which should take Pisana Jelika and Visoka Glava. Just have a look at other highlighted portions, elevations 611 for the 330th Mountain Brigade, 319th Mountain Brigade should attack Hajducka Kosa, SDB, and others elevations 732 [sic]. This is ordered on the 30th of August, 1994. Judge Lattanzi asked then PW-9, on 5601, transcript page, line 8 to 12 on the 15th of November: "The plan that the El Mujahedin Detachment prepared independently, was it approved by the units that were hierarchically above the EMD? PW-9 replied: "Once the operation had been planned, the command or the commander of Operations Group 3 North was informed." Operations Group 3 North, between the 20th of August and afterwards, is informed that there is a plan from the El Mujahedin Detachment. And eight days after the decision for attack, we see here Exhibit 838. And I ask Your Honours to remember the features. Hajducka Kosa, highlighted here, is obviously taken because it refers to "yesterday": "On the 22nd of August," the first word, "yesterday, on the 22nd of August, there were offensive combat operations." And what does the report say? "We broke through the Chetnik lines of defence and reached the line between," and so on. Then the positions are listed, Hajducka Kosa, K-734. I have highlighted this to Your Honours. These are the other units. That is the SDB who took K-734, and dugout was captured in the K-611 sector. I have highlighted this, Your Honours. Another unit was supposed to take this sector. And units of the EMD successfully took control of both features specified in the task, Pisana Jelika and Visoka Glava. And, please pay attention to the last sentence: The 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade is linking up with the EMD on a new line. There is each unit achieving its goal, as ordered seven days ago; and the 7th Muslim Brigade, at least, is linking up with the El Mujahedin afterwards. This is ARBiH directed combat in the Prosecution's point of view. Paragraph 895, this is a later operation on OG North; again a denial by the Defence. The EMD carried out the action independently when it thought it should do so, despite the 3rd Corps order for joint action with other units. They did not follow, the Defence alleges, the 3rd Corps order regarding the action on Kajin Sopot in October 1994. The previous comment was 27 August 1994. About two months later, denial by the Defence. We say the EMD attacked Kajin Sopot in accordance with ARBiH orders. What happens more than two weeks before the attack on Kajin Sopot, 16th of September, 1994: The 3rd Corps commander orders - that's Exhibit 1128 - that the 3rd Corps engineer battalion is to do something, to resubordinate immediately one pioneer squad of the 3rd Corps engineer battalion to the EMD. For what purpose? The order is clear: For the forthcoming combat operations in the area of responsibility of 3 North, 16th of September, 1994. The post-combat report of 3rd Corps, Your Honours, Exhibit 839 informs you: On 3 October units of the OG 3 North carried out attacks along several axes; number one prominently. The EMD coordination with part -- in coordination with part of forces of the 319th. In August, they fought together. Occupied the features of Kajin Sopot, Previja, and Brdo. Just want to focus to the last line of the reporting of the 3rd Corps: The units linked up and took positions along the new line of defence. Again, a link up between the units after the combat: Kajin Sopot, Previja, and Brdo, Your Honours. We believe that is clear. In conclusion, I just want to move out. I want to refer to a statement of Mr. Awad, referring to the El Mujahedin Detachment or the Mujahedin from Poljanice: "We would have a small sector for attacking," Mr. Awad told Your Honours," but we cannot do it alone. When 100 men enters a forest, a wood, they can cover not even 50 metres, not to mention a kilometre or more." What does that mean? The El Mujahedin Detachment alone could not do it. They were subordinated, in our view, because any convert with hundred of men. If Your Honours think about Maline, how can you take with 50, 60 -- I don't want to give a precise number. The unit was being built up. How can you take with a few men an area such Maline, such as Guca Gora. You cannot do it alone. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours, once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would first like to explain to you how the Defence intends to present its closing arguments on behalf of General Rasim Delic. Unlike the Prosecution, we will first be dealing with the issues related to command responsibility over the so-called Poljanice group and the El Mujahedin Detachment. I will be speaking about command responsibility in this case, and I will also deal with the purported assessment of the availability to the Trial Chamber; and my colleague Mr. Robson will speak about the relate events from June 1993, including the requirements from Article 7(3) of the Statute, and the crime base related to July and September 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I hope you are not going to repeat what is in the final brief; however, if you can concentrate mainly on the questions raised by the Bench, that would be very helpful.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will be focussing on the questions asked by the Trial Chamber, and I will focus on those questions or -- yes, on those questions that require an answer in light of the Prosecution brief. As regards the questions, Your Honours, let me explain that I will be dealing with some of the questions, my learned colleague Mr. Robson with others; and I will be answering those questions in the context of my closing arguments, if you allow me to do so. Your Honours, it is a great responsibility to stand here and to present a closing arguments before you after almost a year of trial time because so much is at stake. Now we're in a situation where the Trial Chamber is going to withdraw to deliberate, and what we expect from you is justice. We do not expect and we do not call for an acquittal that would be influenced by any factor that goes beyond this case. The facts in this case speak for themselves, and they speak clearly in favour of such a verdict. The Prosecution approach to this case was to generalise matters. Its theory, its case, was and, indeed, remains unclear. From the very beginning, the case was uncompelling. It is also unfounded. They construed and constructed facts. They used fabricated orders to bring General Rasim Delic into the dock. Your Honours, you will remember the purported orders for the attack on Vozuca on the 16th and 17th of July, 1995, Exhibits 496 and 494; and you will recall the purported order for an attack on the same area on the 26th of August, 1995. Your Honours, those orders did not exist, and we explained that. The Prosecution gives different interpretation or meaning to the documents because those who -- their own witnesses give a completely different interpretation. And, here, invoke Exhibit 400, the plan of the coordination of the General Staff of the ARBiH for September 1995; and Exhibit 600, the plan for the coordination of General Staff for August 1995; and the comments made by Witness Sead Delic, 20th of September 2007, transcript page 2735; and Ismet Alija, the date is 16th of October, 2007, transcript page 4137, in relation to those documents. When the Prosecution lacks arguments, it resorts to mistranslation. Although it is aware of the fact that the translation is erroneous --

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is it okay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down a little bit, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. So when the Prosecution lacks arguments, it resorts to mistranslation. Although it is aware of the fact that the translation is wrong, and although it was duty-bound to remove the mistranslated documents from the record, because transcripts have made it clear that this is what it was, a mistranslation. And, here, I refer to Exhibits 444, where key words from the documents such as, for instance, the word "obracanje," addressed by General Delic, was translated as instructions; E-25, the word that you were able to see yesterday, "staresina," senior officer, was translated as commander; and E-364, the word "posijetjo," visited, was translated as inspected. This is by no means an exhaustive list. This happened every time when we were dealing with a key document for this case, and every time it had a direct link with Rasim Delic. This is the way in which the Prosecution has tried to construct their case. That's not a case at all. This is just an illusion, and we believe that the Trial Chamber will reject those arguments. We believe that the Trial Chamber will not apply the legal theory whereby the accused, who was, as the Prosecution allegations, at the top of the hierarchy, which included the El Mujahedin Detachment, should be convicted simply because he was at the top of this hierarchy. The Honourable Trial Chamber may convict our client only if it manages to find a direct and specific nexus of the incidents that are charged with the accused and his specific knowledge of the crimes, not of crimes committed by just anyone, but crimes committed by his subordinates. Evidence called in this case do not support this. Before I move on to some specific issues related to command responsibility, I would like to say something about the suggestions made by the Prosecution related to the approach that you should take in evaluating evidence. Paragraphs 10 through 16 of the Prosecution final brief, it is -- the Prosecution actually gives you advice how to assess the credibility of the witnesses, presenting a series of insinuations about the witnesses that are not appropriate for a criminal court. For instance, the Prosecution says some witnesses tell the truth about some things, and they could not tell the truth about some other things. Some exaggerate in certain aspects of their testimony, either because of their role or the role of their family in the war. Which witnesses are we talking about? What things that they tell the truth or do not tell the truth about? What aspects? Whose aspects of whose testimony? We don't know that. We were not told. In the courtroom here, we did not hear a single word about anyone's involvement or the involvement of anyone's family in the events of the war. The Prosecution did not call any evidence about that. No questions of this nature were ever asked of any of the witnesses. So what is the Prosecution talking about? The Defence, Your Honours, does not know that. If the Trial Chamber were to adopt the approach that the Prosecution wants it to, it would really sink very low. It would indeed hit rock bottom, and this Trial Chamber, I'm sure, will not allow itself to do so. The Prosecution talks about many witnesses, ARBiH members who spoke about foreign fighters, about BH army members who are still serving or who have been recently retired; paragraph 14. The Defence called many witnesses; indeed, more than half of its witnesses did not speak about any foreign fighters. Only one Defence witness is still active, not in the army, but in the Ministry of Defence. None of the Defence witnesses have retired recently. So, as far as I can see, the Prosecution invites you not to believe its own witnesses. The Prosecutors tell you that they gave evidence about foreign fighters, El Mujahedin Detachment members, in order to put some distance between the BH army and the serious crimes in which members of this detachment were involved; and they tell you that even though those members of the El Mujahedin Detachment, six of them who took the stand as Prosecution witnesses, were never asked any questions about involvement in those crimes, their involvement, or the involvement of their fellow fighters from the detachment. Now they invite you to take the sword of injustice into your hands and to cut out those segments from the transcripts and the evidence of most of the Prosecution witnesses to find the accused guilty. They want you to set aside a huge number of substantial exculpatory evidence presented by those witnesses for a very simple reason: They do not have an answer to those facts. Their only answer is they were, or they still are, members of the BH army and they are not to be trusted, except when their evidence supports the charges. One guesses, then, that at that time, they're telling the truth. I ask myself what universe does the Prosecution live in if it believe this is this is an appropriate approach to a criminal trial? How can the Prosecution suggest to you that you should not trust the witnesses that they called to testify before you under oath? How can they suggest to you that you should not believe what their witnesses say, yet they never try to the impeach those witnesses, at all; and they did not do that for any of their witnesses. If they thought those witnesses were not telling the truth under oath, they were under a professional obligation to call them to task immediately, yet they never did that. In other words, they believed them. Now they don't like the outcome of their testimony, and they invite you not to put any trust in them. Even if you wanted to do what the Prosecution has suggested you should do, you would put yourself in an unenviable situation, a serious situation, indeed, because it would have legal consequences. This is a situation where it is not only about whether you should believe or not believe their witnesses. What this is all about is that the Defence had the right to take into account the facts that the Prosecution witnesses testified about certain issues and that the Prosecution did not attempt to impeach or discredit those witnesses. We were completely entitled to decide not to call some evidence because those issues were explained by their own witnesses and it was not challenged. That's what we did. Were that not the case, Your Honours, you would have seen 50 Defence witnesses before this Court, given the fact that the Prosecutor on various occasions challenged the credibility of their own witnesses. You have your witnesses and yet you don't lent them credence. This is something that the jurisprudence has already dealt with in the Brdjanin case on the 24th of January, 2002, page 805. The Trial Chamber drew the following conclusion: If at any point during his testimony a witness turns on you and disrupts your plans with that witness as one's own witness, then evidently you're facing a very difficult situation. You will no longer be allowed to impeach the witness before you obtain the Chamber's permission to do so. This same approach was taken by the Trial Chamber in its oral decision in the Limaj case on the 1st of February, 2005. At no point in time did the Prosecutor try to seek the Chamber's leave to declare a witness hostile. I can't call upon you now to view their own witnesses as not credible. I can't ask you to not believe them. They didn't impeach those witnesses, and they didn't declare them hostile. Why, Your Honours? Because you, the Chamber, would then have heard the sordid truth about the investigation behind this trial. You would have heard what the witnesses had to go through and what methods the OTP used in obtaining evidence in order to be -- in order to be able to raise this indictment. Their witnesses or, for that matter, the Defence witness from their list, did, after all, tell you a thing or two about the Prosecutor's modus operandi. Karahasanovic, on the 4th of April 2008, page 8135, describes his interview with an OTP investigator about the perpetrators: "Yes. I did say that a group of Arabs arrived. He then asked me whether the unit was the El Mujahid Unit. I said I didn't know," yet he was adamant - excuse me - that this was the El Mujahid Unit because "that was the only unit around," as he said, "which meant that it couldn't possibly have been anyone else." Your Honours, yesterday, they used the statement taken from Izet Karahasanovic to buttress their own evidence, but they failed to say how they obtained that evidence. They were adamant that he should say the El Mujahedin Detachment, although the man was actually saying Arabs. Although they have that list which they have made ample use of as evidence, where he entered into his own handwriting the following wording: "Those people were taken by the Arabs," and "the Arabs" was the word used, not the El Mujahid Detachment. Husic, describing his interview with Investigator Koehler, on the 14th of March, 2008, page 7579: "He told me, among other things, that anyone who spent four years in a war might find himself caught up in a situation where others were asking themselves what his possible involvement might have been. I felt that this was a kind of threat, and that is why I refused to go on working with them." Husic, again on the 14th of March, 2008, page 7578, describes the way in which the Prosecutor drew up his statement. He said: "It is frustrating for me, but I don't see here the questions that I was then asked. They were not included in the statement, and my answer was placed in a different context of other questions that are now being asked." Zilkic, on the 13th of November, 2007, page 5408, explains the discrepancy between the evidence given to the Prosecutor and in court. He says: "They said some things and they expected certain answers. Was it like this? Was it not like this? Perhaps I said this? Perhaps I said that? But, I believe, that at least to some extent, this was forcing my hand." My question was: "Forcing your hand, what do you mean? Answer: "I was coerced into making a statement. My hands were tied. I had no choice." On the 25th of September, 2007, in response to the Prosecutor's request that written statements be admitted under Rule 92 ter, we described to you the risk, the risk being that such evidence was not obtained in a fair and proper way. We described several examples. One of the witness was literally told by the Prosecutor: "I see a smile on your face; and I think that if you read something like this, it is really repulsive what they did to someone who fought for the BH army and who did his best for Bosnia and Herzegovina." Your Honours, they adopted the most atrocious means in order to influence witnesses, the most atrocious and cruelest means; and that is why the Prosecutor decided to bear their time waiting for the witness in this case to turn their backs before they said that those witnesses should not be trusted. Had that not been the case, these are the answers they would have heard. The Prosecutor chose their own witnesses, despite the fact that they had heard many other witnesses they could have brought here, ranging from top-ranking politicians to religious figures. Be that as it may, Your Honours, the most important thing is this: The Prosecutor now suggests that their own witnesses were not telling the truth about the relations between the BH army and the El Mujahid Detachment. But that is simply not true. It wasn't just members of the BH army that gave evidence about this. There were several groups of witnesses that talked about control that was exercised over the Mujahedin, generally speaking, in the El Mujahedin Detachment. First of all, members of the BH army, and that is who the Prosecutor is talking about. The following group is members of the El Mujahid Detachment: Six of them, one of them Arab; and then there was a Croat witness who had nothing to do with the El Mujahid Detachment or the BH army for that matter; and, finally, Your Honours, Croat and Serb victims themselves. Yesterday, the Prosecutor showed two slides that had to do with witness evidence. Both of the witnesses in question describe a situation that Your Honours will no doubt remember: Members of the BH army were doing their best to keep the Mujahedin from gaining access to the prisoners; or rather, they did their best to protect them from the Mujahedin. Based on all this evidence, including the evidence given by victims, there is but one conclusion that is possible. The BH army commands were in control neither of the Mujahedin, nor of the El Mujahid Detachment specifically. The OTP are telling you exactly what the Defence are trying to prove. The El Mujahid Detachment was out of control. What they're saying, however, is a form of revisionism. That is why they are advising you to be cautious. The first question, Your Honours, is this: How can the Prosecutor reconcile this statement with much of the evidence found at the Islamic Cultural Centre in Milan? This evidence is derived from a completely neutral source. It offers incontrovertible truth on who controlled the Mujahedin across the Bosnia and the El Mujahid Detachment specifically, and how. Based on these documents, it is clear that they were not under the control of the BH army, and least of all under the command of General Rasim Delic. Exhibit 394 [as interpreted]. Could we please look at Exhibit 394 -- 1394. This is a fax sent by the El Mujahid Detachment to the Islamic Cultural Centre in Milan, 7th of March, 1995.

utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a fax message, dated the 7th of March, 1995, sent to the Islamic Cultural Centre in Milan. The El Mujahid Detachment explains its relationship to the BH army: "When the detachment was established and recognised by the BH army, the recognition did not necessarily mean acceptance. That is what they said. However, speaking of this theory of revisionism, I wish to say that this is something that is beyond the bounds of this case, and I'm convinced that the Chamber will not pay this the slightest heed. The Chamber has the evidence right there, no more and no less. The OTP have no right to talk about history. They have no right to talk about revisionism, not as far as the BH army is concerned. It has already put into the dock several high-ranking officers of the BH army. The verdicts speak for themselves. What exactly do they tell us? Your Honours, look at the transcript. They would normally quote a number of lotions to a witness and then ask them to link them up by using arrows. "Question: In actual fact, you weren't with the Arabs at all at the time, were you? "Answer: No, I wasn't. "Question: You weren't able to observe their movements? "Answer: No. We simply heard about the directions or axes along which they were moving, but I didn't see this for myself." Sinan Begovic, therefore, heard about their movements, directions or axes. That is what he said, and yet, here, you have a map where the same Sinan Begovic actually draws this based on hearsay. The OTP tell us that they led evidence about how documents were sent or received. In actual fact, many documents were shown to witnesses, many documents were used in the OTP's final brief, E-658 E-641, E-111, E-797, that witnesses described as drafts, mere drafts. There were many documents that witnesses clearly described as not reflecting the reality. Jusic, a Prosecution witness, on the 19th of September, 2007, commented on Exhibit 111, and said: "I can't be shown anything that would change my mind, regardless of what I see written here. I know and I believe that they caused nothing but damage. They should have never come to Bosnia in the first place. So if this is meant to refute what I said, then this in no way affects me. I have read what is written here, and I disagree with 80 per cent of this statement praising the El Mujahedin Detachment." This was one of their own witnesses. There were many documents that witnesses described as never implemented. Sljuka, on the 23rd of October, for example: "I can't remember all the orders pursuant to which the El Mujahid Detachment arrive in the area of responsibility of the 35th Division. However, when I talking about this, I meant no more than the following: I meant that the El Mujahid Detachment failed to comply with the orders given by the commander of the 35th Division." He was unable to exercise command over this unit. This again, is something that was stated by an OTP witness, a member of the 35th Division. In fact, although we challenge the authenticity of many of the documents, the Prosecution never tried to prove their authenticity or chain of custody. In lieu of that, the Prosecution tendered into evidence Exhibit 924, a statement made by Mr. Sadinlija, the head of the BH army archives. And when you read this statement, you will learn that Mr. Sadinlija, in fact, does not know anything about what happened to the documents until his arrival to the archives as the head. You will learn much about the way that the Prosecutors seized those documents. In paragraph 27, Your Honours, you will find that Mr. Sadinlija said: The archives personnel were asked to leave the room where documents were being inspected, and the personnel complied. This is what Mr. Sadinlija said: "They asked us to leave the premises of the archives while they inspected the documents, and we complied." Again, in paragraph 31, you will see that in 2003, the entire Tuzla archive was removed and that the originals have never been returned to the BH army archives. Paragraph 39 tells us that a huge number of documents were inspected and that, at the end, the archives -- the archive merely received a list of those documents. And, finally, that Investigator Koehler did not ask for any determination of the authenticity of either the documents or the list. Your Honours, you have had an opportunity to look at Exhibit 165, tendered through Witness PW-3; and then all of a sudden we have the same document now, as Exhibit 378, with a chart showing the position of the El Mujahedin Detachment within the 3rd Corps, and this was given another exhibit number, 379. The Prosecutor used this document and refers to it in paragraph 98 of its final brief; although, if you look at the last page of this document, you can see that this document has a completely different attachment. And you can also see that this document was not authenticated by Mr. Sadinlija or any person that Mr. Sadinlija designates as his predecessor, in paragraph 10, Exhibit 924. Although, Witness Jusic, said that this chart contains a lot of mistakes, and that this is not part of this document. That is on the 17th of September, 1995, transcript page 2481. Your Honours, perhaps this will be a convenient time to make a break, and then I will continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I was talking about some documents. Of course, it is very important to know what the documents really said about the documents [sic], because you, Your Honours, don't know anything about those documents. You don't know what the actual background was for the creation of those documents, whether the contents are accurate fully or partially or whether they're completely inaccurate. That is why we have witnesses. If it weren't like that, all the parties would have to do would be to just mail the document, write down their theories of the case, and mail those theories and then await the judgement. That is why what the Prosecutor is asking you to do is not serious at all. They quote the Stakic judgement, claiming that it is based almost entirely on documents, and Prosecution also invokes some other cases, such as for instance, the Brdjanin case. But in doing so, the Prosecution paints a completely wrong picture. The approach the OTP took in those cases was completely different, as was in all the other cases before this Tribunal. The Prosecution called the investigators and the archive personnel to testify about the origin of the document, the chain of custody, the production of documents, authenticity, and all the other issues that are related to authenticity; and this was subject to the cross-examination by the Defence. Exhibit 924, Mr. Sadinlija's statement, was of no assistance in this respect. The Prosecution expects you to be believe, to take its word, that their documents are accurate, reliable, and authentic; although, as regards the facts contained in the documents, the witnesses provided a completely different interpretation or, in some cases, those very documents were challenged by other documents. In paragraph 19 of its final brief, the OTP explains that its case is based on circumstantial evidence. The metaphor that was used is that the Prosecution case is not just an ordinary chain where the whole chain breaks. If one link breaks, it is actually chain-mail. So, even if one link breaks, the strength of the chain-mail remains the same. And I will use another metaphor. I will say that their case is just a huge patch work made of pieces of cloth from various pieces of clothing. You take one patch from here, another patch from there, using different fabrics. Imagine that those fabrics are different documents from which the Prosecutor selected parts that were in his favour. What they did is a jigsaw puzzle that makes no sense. You would have to set aside this huge pile of fabric that they discarded to conclude that this patchwork paints a full picture. You would have to set aside this pile of fabrics to conclude that they have managed to prove any of the counts in the indictment beyond reasonable doubt. In its final brief, the Prosecution did not say anything about the background of this case. What the Prosecution has presented you with is a narrow frame, and it is asking you to ignore everything that happened outside of this frame. If you were to adopt this approach, the Prosecution approach, you would not have enough information necessary for you to assess the facts appropriately, to apply law to the situation that the accused found himself in. Law related to command responsibility and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal has recognised the vital importance of what was happening in the theatre of war in the relevant time. And, here, I refer to a decision of the Appeals Chamber on the interlocutory appeal of the Defence against the length of the trial, the date is the 20th of July, 2005, Oric case. In this case, the Delic case, this is of particular importance because this is a case involving a high-ranking commander. Before you, Your Honours, you have the commander of the General Staff whose basic duty was to implement the mission of the General Staff. This was the strategic level of command, not dealing with individual units and problems. For General Delic, what was at stake was the survival of the people and the Bosnia and Herzegovina. The Prosecution never went into the background of this case; and what we see in background is tens of thousands of people killed, thousands of women raped, children evens, hundreds of thousands of Muslims expelled from their homes, and not only Muslims but other people who were loyal to the BiH government. That's the story that remained untold. Had you heard this story, Your Honours, after the end of the Prosecution case, and during our opening statement held on the 4th of March, 2008, page 6914 of the transcript, you would not have asked this question. If I can ask you, if we don't have an army that is under control, why go into the war at all? You will find an answer to that question when you look at this exhibit, Exhibit 80.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, please remember the shell fired from the Mount Ozren that killed 71 persons in Tuzla; Exhibit 471 and Exhibit 625. Organised or unorganised, the army had to accept battle, and what a battle it was, the one between David and Goliath. You will have it bear those facts in mind when you deliberate, not only because of the significant of the background of this case, and not only because General Delic had to have dealt with those problems, because he did. You will have to bear this fact in mind because the problems and internal conflict that General Delic faced had a major impact, a direct impact on the effectiveness of the chain of command and the possibility to establish a normal flow of information through the chain of command, and the possibility of establishing effective control. This is what you heard from various witnesses, Karavelic, Loncaric, Dedovic, Jusic, Softic, Buljabasic, Alihodzic, and others. What the Prosecution termed the core of its case. It told you a simple story about Muslim extremists who came to Central Bosnia, then to murder. They killed people. That's what they said. They killed people, and Rasim Delic flew about that. He knew about the crimes, yet they rewarded them and he praised them in the media. This, despite the fact that we did not see any of this in the evidence, Your Honours. The Prosecutor played the card that any reasonable person must find alien: Muslim extremists bent on killing civilians came to Central Bosnia. The people who did come to Central Bosnia were not all the same. They were not all bent on killing non-Bosniak civilians or prisoners of war. This is a figment of the Prosecution's fantasy. Your Honours, I invite to you look at testimony of Witness DW-4, at pages 4471 to 4427. He described a group of Arabs who were under his command and who were normal and disciplined people. Awad, their witness, the witness that they referred to in their final brief so often, told the Trial Chamber that the El Mujahedin Detachment had been set up specifically so that they could distance themselves from other groups that did not comply with discipline. And this is from Awad's testimony on the 9th of February, 2008, transcript at pages 154, 155. If what Awad said were -- or, rather, Exhibit 1200 clearly shows that Awad was right. It was a bulletin of the El Mujahedin Detachment sent abroad on the 6th of March, 1995, which reads as follows: "Likewise, the Mujahedin relations and their movements are a function of what may safeguard the legitimacy of the Jihad and its special nature, and the detachment has made it clear several times that they refused to take responsibility for acts and infractions by individuals or groups that do not belong to it." We expect you not to take into account this fashionable story of Muslim extremists, killings, this indefinite and unclear danger looming over every prisoner of war in Central Bosnia that falls into their hands. I will go back to the beginning of the story the Prosecution told about the Muslim extremists who came to Central Bosnia. Their arrival in Central Bosnia, their joining to the Muslim Forces in Travnik, and their control over them were described in their final brief with few words and many photographs depicting bearded men, as if we hadn't seen each and every one of them at least ten times during the trial. All these people of Arab origin were bundled together into the Poljanice group. According to the OTP, all of them automatically became members of the El Mujahid Detachment; and all of them, no more and no less, even prior to the establishment of the El Mujahedin Detachment, were under the de facto control of Rasim Delic. This is a far cry from what was actually the case. It is also a far cry from the evidence in this trial. There were numerous and very diverse groups of Mujahedin fighting and throughout the area. They were many humanitarian workers of Afro-Asian origins, as well. We have provided detailed description of evidence about the Prosecutor's confused pleading in relation to effective control over the Mujahedin prior to these establishment of the detachment, and the detachment itself, in paragraphs 99 through 180 of our final brief, and I'm not going back to that now. One thing I will tell you, though, is as far as this issue is concerned, the Prosecution invokes witness Hamad. The OTP rely, to a very large extent, on his evidence. We realised that yesterday. This, Your Honours, is a witness who actually said that the military commanders of the Mujahedin, Vahidin and Muatez, were members of al-Qaeda, and that was the organisation that they reported to. That is what their star witness said, Ali Ahmad Ali Hamad, on the 8th of September. The transcript reference is pages 101 and 102. He says: "Question: In relation to that, Witness, I want to ask you this. It is true, isn't it, that you, the Mujahedin who were members of al-Qaeda, and you have accepted that as a fact, haven't you, were under the control of Wahiuddin, were monitored by Wahiuddin, and that he wrote reports about you to his bosses? Am I right? "Answer: Yes. "Question: These are the al-Qaeda bosses, right. "Answer: Yes. "Question: Therefore, it would be fair to say that the Mujahedin administration submitted reports on activities of the Mujahedin in Bosnia and their members to leaders or bosses outside of Bosnian. "Answer: Correct." That's what Ali Ahmad Ali Hamad said. In our brief, we listed specifically a lot of evidence that testifies to this, and I'm not going back to that now. What I am going to deal with now is how the Prosecutor in this case pleaded the criminal responsibility of the accused and what they have actually proven. In paragraph 15 of the indictment, they plead that General Rasim Delic, as the commander of the Main Staff, had supreme authority and supreme responsibility for the functioning of the BH army. In paragraph 17, they list the units under his effective control, including the El Mujahedin Detachment. In paragraph 761 through 834 of our final brief, we provide a detailed explanation to the effect that the Prosecutor is relying on regulations that did not apply at all at the time these events occurred. We also provided a detailed explanation of the accused's actual position. Again, I'm not going back to that. There is, however, a material fact that shows a relationship of subordination between the perpetrators in question and the accused. The Prosecutor pleads that Rasim Delic on the 16th and 17th of July 1995, paragraph 30 of the indictment, and on the 26th of August, 1995, paragraph 31 of the indictment, ordered to the 2nd and 3rd Corps to carry out combat operations in the Vozuca pocket. In paragraph 19.3 of their pre-trial brief, they explain that Delic was there command of these operations by using the El Mujahedin Detachment. Finally, they plead that he ordered a cessation of those combat operations; paragraph 32 of the indictment. Your Honours, these facts were the foundation of the indictment against Rasim Delic. That was the foundation, and the OTP failed to prove that. We go on to explain that in section 6 and 7 of our final brief. Why am I saying this today? The OTP are perfectly aware of the fact that they have failed to prove the material facts that they pleaded. Now, in their final brief, they place before you a new set of facts. Now, the nexus between the accused and the developments in the July 1995, as well as the perpetrators of those crimes, is described in paragraph 63 of their final brief. They submit that Rasim Delic ordered to the BH army corps to activate the entire front line of the BH army. The link between the accused and what happened during Operation Farz is now described in the following way. They now claim that the General Staff secured instructions at a strategic level; and that Rasim Delic, in a directive for 1995 as one of the tasks for the 2nd and 3rd Corps, assigned coordination of efforts to liberate Vozuca. This is paragraph 86 of the OTP's final brief. Your Honours, that is not what they initially pleaded. Nevertheless, you have the indictment in front of you, and you will have to provide your own findings in relation to the allegations contained in that indictment, as opposed to what they're telling us now. Your Honours, I am moving closer to my answer to your question number 5. As far as the relationship of subordination is concerned, in paragraphs 41, 42, and 49 of their final brief, the OTP tell us that the Mujahedin from Poljanice, prior to the establishment of the detachment, were de facto subordinated to General Delic; whereas, after the establishment of the detachment, they were de jure subordinated to the 3rd Corps and thereby to Rasim Delic as the BH army commander. They claim that it is of no consequence whether this relationship of subordination was direct or indirect. I do agree, but under the condition that they cite the following as well: Only for as long as the accused remains in effective control of the perpetrators. Finally, I'm getting to question number 5. Your Honours wanted to know whether it was the position of the Defence that Rasim Delic could be made to answer under Article 7(3) of the Statute, only for as long as he, as you said, directly and with no intercession by any of the units or formations exercised command over the unit that committed the crimes that we are talking about. Of course not, Your Honours. Of course, that is not the position of the Defence, as we clearly explain in paragraph 792, where we elaborate on the importance of the principle of singleness of command in the BH army; in paragraph 793, where we elaborate on the various levels of command in the BH army, including the strategic level, as well as the responsibility of commanders at all levels of command, as well as their mutual relationships. We would like you to look at paragraph 921 of the Defence's final brief, in which we clearly state our position in relation to the issue that you raised. The OTP had to prove that the chain of command was functioning, starting from the accused and then all the way down the chain to the alleged perpetrators of these crimes. The Trial Chamber must establish, beyond reasonable doubt, that any action taken by the accused, portrayed by the OTP as establishing effective control, qualifies as unequivocal exercise of power by the accused. This is in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal. This is Celebici, paragraph 669. In paragraph 852 of our final brief, we state that the authority of a superior officer requires for a de facto chain of command to exist, functioning from the top down and vis-a-versa, between the accused and the alleged perpetrators at the time the crime cured. And this is also in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal; Celebici paragraph 674. The threshold of effective control is a factual situation reflected in the ability of the accused to enforce compliance with the rules and with his own orders by his subordinate officers. And let me try to be very specific about your question number 5. His control exercised directly over the perpetrators or through other subordinate officers down the chain of command from him, but up the chain of command from them. This is entirely insignificant, as long as the responsible superior officer has the means to prevent any crimes from occurring, or, indeed, has the means to take appropriate measures to punish the perpetrators. This is also reflected in the jurisprudence of the Tribunal; Oric case, paragraph 311. That is our position. That is why we used paragraph 891 of our brief, and we took it from there trying to decipher that the subordinate officers of General Delic and the commander of certain commands, including the command of the 3rd Corps and the 35th Division, had no de facto power over the El Mujahedin Detachment. That is why we devoted an entire chapter to factors that undermined the chain of command in the area covered by the 35th Division. This is something that we described in your final brief. In relation to this, Your Honours, I also wish to draw your attention to paragraph 197 of the Appeals Chamber judgement in the Celebici trial, stating: "The doctrine of command responsibility is finally established based on the power of a superior officer to control, the actions of his subordinates. According to this judgement, there is a certain threshold after which persons no longer have the necessary control over those who committed crimes, and may therefore not be considered in any true sense of the word "their superior officers" under Article 7(3) of the Statute. While any Trial Chamber must always take into account specific facts of any situation, while any Trial Chamber must be prepared to penetrate through countless veils of formalities behind which individuals perhaps are hiding who bear the greatest possibly responsibility for a number of atrocities, one must be cautious not to be unjust or inequitable towards people who are declared responsible for actions that were maybe committed by others in situations where this control length was simple non-exist or was simply far to remote. The OTP claim that judging the fact whether Rasim Delic was, in fact, part of a subordination relationship would depend on indicators and factors that they state in paragraph 46 of their final brief. If you look at these factors, Your Honours, you will reach the conclusion that the OTP are trying to prove that the BH army, in fact, had effective control over the El Mujahedin Detachment, not General Delic. This is what we're talking about. It is effective control that's at stake, the effective control of General Delic over the perpetrators of crimes. They claim that he had effective control over the detachment, and they base there claim on the fact that he issued orders on the establishment and disbanding of the detachment. Your Honours, we studied this issue in quite some detail in paragraph 835 through 968 of our final brief. In the briefest possible terms, I will say that none of those orders, in fact, stems from his position of authority. Quite the contrary, it stems from the authority of his superior officer. Those orders were merely handed down the chain of command. That is one aspect of the establishment of the El Mujahedin Detachment. There are others, too, Your Honours, and you have seen the evidence. In paragraphs 972 through 1016, we tell you who the real founders of the detachment are, and describe the existence of other authorities who had power over the detachment, including the Islamic Cultural Centre in Milan and Sheikh Anwar Saban. We describe an entirely independent and military system that backed the unit and that the unit was part of. In our brief, paragraphs 937 through 967, we talk about evidence that has to do with incentives. This is about General Delic, and the OTP deal with this a lot in their own brief. You will remember, Your Honours, the evidence given by Mr. Loncaric, as well as that given by Mr. Husic. They both said that the awarding of those incentives was a result of the political decision that lay beyond the bounds of Rasim Delic's authority. Rasim Delic never proposed any ranks for members of the El Mujahedin Detachment. You will remember PW-9's testimony, as well as the fact that not even any decisions of the presidency of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina on ranks were respected by members of the El Mujahedin Detachment or, indeed, recognised by them. This was on the 5th of November 2007; 5644. Your Honours, may I remind you of a widely recognised position, in the jurisprudence, regarding the requirements that must be met by an order, in order to be taken into account when establishing effective control. What must be proven is that an accused was not just simply in a position to issue orders; rather, what must be proven is that those orders are recognised and complied with by the subordinates, or the perpetrators of crimes. This piece of jurisprudence was reflected in the Blaskic Appeals judgement, paragraph 69. So what we're looking for is evidence that the orders of the accused are being obeyed, not only by just anyone, but by the perpetrators of the crimes. The Prosecution must prove that the perpetrator acted because of those orders and in compliance with the orders issued by the accused, not orders of -- by just anyone. This, again, is jurisprudence. This is Nikolic case, a decision on the review of the indictment in relation to Rule 61. The date is the 20th of October, 1995, paragraph 24. Your Honours, this is not the reality in the case of the El Mujahedin Detachment. The Prosecution invoked Witness Awad somewhere in the middle of its final brief and the closing argument. This is what the witness said: "By Allah, had the Shura decide at that time that the detachment would not be disbanded and that it would continue to fight, nobody would have forced us to disband the detachment." As I have already said, Your Honours, the Prosecution listed a number of factors for your consideration in the evaluation of effective control as being indicative of it. You will find very few of those that are actually recognised by the international and humanitarian law and the jurisprudence before this Tribunal that might lead to you conclude that General Delic did have effective control over the El Mujahedin Detachment. Even if the El Mujahedin Detachment had been under the BH army control, as the Prosecution alleges - but that was not the case, that's our case - so even if this detachment had been under BH army control at the time relevant for the indictment, the position of this detachment, which was allegedly resubordinated to the 35th Division, would be too far removed from the commander of the General Staff for him to actually receive reports from the 35th Division. As you were able to see, the reports from the 35th Division regarding this unit never reached General Delic. You saw from voluminous evidence called at this trial that the reports were abridged through different levels of command from the bottom to the top; and that, in the end, General Delic would receive nothing about a brief report, quite general in nature, about certain combat actions. BH army did have its levels of command; and, as we explained, each of the commanders had their subordinates and their responsibilities. Let us now look at the substance of what they're alleging regarding the indicators of effective control. The Prosecution is trying to prove that Rasim Delic did have effective control over the El Mujahedin Detachment by saying that the Mujahedin, the El Mujahedin Detachment, upon its establishment, was involved in the fighting with the BH army in Central Bosnia. And they go on to list various locations, Karaula, Bijelo Bucje, Maline, Hrasce, Djotline Kuce, Vitez, Pisana Jelika, Visoka Glava, Kajin Sopot, and Operations Proljece and Farz. Witnesses, who were members of the detachment, Awad and PW-9, explained in quite some detail that the fighting for Pisana Jelika, Visoka Glava, Kajin Sopot and Proljece was carried out independently. They did not have anything to do with -- the fighting did not have anything to do with the orders of the BH army commands. You will recall, Your Honours, that the reports on those battles were actually sent to the Islamic Cultural Centre in Milan. Let me refer here to E-1201 and E-1387. These are not bulletins. These are combat reports, pure and simple, that describe in great detail this fighting. Those reports were sent to the Islamic Cultural Centre in Milan, not to the BH army commands. Your Honours, whom do you send your reports, anywhere in the world, to your bosses, to your superiors? You don't talk to your superiors. You present your accounts to them, you file written reports. In paragraphs 360 through 385 of our final brief, we provided some arguments related to this fighting, and I had not now go through them again. Let me just show what you the witnesses say about the battles that we did not mention in our brief, and the Prosecution discusses them. Witness Delalic describes the relationship between the BH army and the detachment as one of cooperation. That's the 27th of August, 2007, regarding the battle of Djotline Kuce. I would like to draw your attention the last part of the question asked by His Honour Judge Moloto: "They were in cooperation with you?" And the witness replies: "Probably, probably, at the Djotline Kuce, but I don't know that they actually cooperated with us in such a way that we fought together anywhere." Witness Hamad, regarding Bijelo Bucje says the following. The question is: "In actual fact, during all the time that you spent as the commander of the unit in Bijelo Bucje, you never received a single order from the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; is that correct? Now I'm talking about orders, you personally never received an order from the BH army?" "Not from them. There was only cooperation. There were no orders." PW-2, talking about the battle of Zabige and Kruscica, near Vitez, says that only the detachment took part, nobody else. He says: "I arrived in Zabige as part of another group that was sent in to assist in a way. I saw only members of the El Mujahedin group there, nobody else." PW-2, when he talks about Kruscica, describes an incident in which the detachment arrested a member of the BH army who was not released when the relevant superior command of the army asked that; he was released only when the Travnik mufti, Avdibegovic, intervened: "It is true, is it not, that the soldier was not released when the BH army intervened, but only after Mufti Avdibegovic intervened and that the incident died down after that." "Yes." Your Honours, please bear this fact in find. Mufti Avdibegovic, he is a religious leader and he exerts influence over the Mujahedin, and this is when the situation calms down. The BH army was unable to obtain the release of its own soldier, the soldier that had been arrested. Your Honours, could we please move into private session for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what the witnesses had to say about defining the objectives by the superiors from the BH army and the approving of the plans on their part. Awad, the witness that the Prosecution keeps invoking, explained that: "Shura discussed the plan and then decided whether to launch an attack or not. In other words, the Shura considered and discussed the attack plan, in other words whether a back would be launched or not, am I right? "Answer: Yes. "Question: Likewise, Shura decided about any major issues that touched upon the life and work of the detachment. Is that correct? "Answer: That's correct." PW-9 explained that the detachment was not interested in the plans of the 35th Division. That was on the 16th of November 2007. The transcript page is 56 -- 5706. As regards the indicators the Prosecution talks about in its final brief, resubordination, combat reconnaissance, joint training, the logistics for the detachment, temporary staffing by personnel from the BH army in the detachment, artillery support, conduct in battle and after battle, including holding the lines, the assignment of areas or sectors to EMD, alleged payments effected by the BH army, including certificates and citizenship, we went through all this in detail in sections 5,6,7, and 8-B of our brief, and I will not go through it again. Let us look at what the Prosecution insider witnesses had to say about how this functioned de facto. This is what Awad had to say about setting some conditions. He said: "We would never have launched any attack if conditions had not been met." He explained that the 35th Division or the 3rd Corps could not count on the detachment when they considered that the detachment's engagement would be necessary or when the detachment was actually ordered to do something. This is what Witness PW-9 has to say about the resubordination orders. "You have seen those three documents and a number of other documents and I would like to put my case to you now. Documents that came from the 3rd Corps and the orders that the 3rd Corps used to try to incorporate the El Mujahedin Detachment into the corps structure were just there on paper. The detachment never recognised those orders or any kind of resubordination." "Answer: That's correct." PW-9 says that's correct. Now this is what witness Awad has to say about resubordination. He said: "We would be resubordinated to them in formal terms but none of those commanders could issue any direct orders to us. This just never happened." "Let us clear this up. When you say, 'We would be resubordinated to them in formal terms but none of them could issue any orders to us,' that means that there were orders. There would be a paper, a piece of paper, yet the detachment did not recognise their orders. Is that correct?" "Answer: Yes." Your Honours, at this point I would like to touch upon some inaccuracies that were presented by the Prosecution in its brief. In paragraph 137, the Prosecution notes that the El Mujahedin was used as an intervention rapid reaction unit and that it was used to arrest people, among other things. They referred to a number of exhibits in this paragraph, and I invite to you look at those exhibits, because none of those documents actually show that what the Prosecution is claiming is correct. The Prosecution is incorrect when it claims that the BH army and the El Mujahedin Detachment used the same joint forward command post. This is what their witness Hasanagic said on the 27th of September, 2007. "Here it is stated that you designated a team of your officers, including Nesad Sabic, the Chief of Staff, to provide assistance to the detachment. It says here that you ordered for some assistance to be provided."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "But it is true, Mr. Hasanagic, is it not, Mr. Hasanagic, that the El Mujahedin Detachment never allowed Mr. Sabic to enter their camp. Is that true?" "Answer: This is what my Chief of Staff told me." They simply did not accept your assistance or the assistance of your officers. Am I right?" "Answer: Yes. I would like to say something about the level of professionalism in the OTP. The Prosecution tendered documents E-1146, E-1148, E-1165, E-1167, E-1169, through the bar table, and used those documents, allegedly on the basis of those documents, the Prosecution put together table number 4 attached to its final brief. In paragraphs 161 and 162, the Prosecution claims that the 3rd Corps commander personally approved the transfers of soldiers whose names are listed in those documents, claiming that you can actually find them in Exhibit 65. Of course, you can't find them there, and you can't find them on the -- all of them on the February 1996 list either. What the Prosecution did was to extract the names that are on the February 1996 list and put them into the table, although most of the people listed in those exhibits are not on this list at all. You will remember many witnesses --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I just interrupt. You're saying what the Prosecution did was to extract the names that are on the February 1996 list and put them. Do we have any evidence to this effect from the trial?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, what I said is this. Not during the trial. The OTP tendered E-1146, E-1148, E-1165, and other documents as bar table exhibits. And then there was a list dated February from which they -- if you go back to the documents that they invoke, you will realise that only the occasional person from that list is mentioned in these exhibits, but certainly not in Exhibit 65, which is the exhibit that they invoke. Your Honours, you will remember many witnesses talking about E-591, where General Mahmuljin bans any further reinforcement to the El Mujahedin Detachment. Be that as it may, Your Honours, but it is precisely the theory of the OTP from paragraph 161 to the effect that the El Mujahid Detachment negotiated with President Izetbegovic about transfers and that General Mahmuljin then personally took the decision on that, tells us better than anything else that Rasim Delic, even according to the OTP, had no effective control over the El Mujahedin Detachment. What is this supposed to mean? The presidency talks directly to the El Mujahedin Detachment and then the commander of the 3rd Corps carries this out. Where is Rasim Delic's place in all of this? Where is it, even according to the OTP? The OTP use up an entire chapter, their chapter on effective control, paragraphs 146 to 150, to convince you that the detachment followed orders of the commands of the BH army. What they had to prove was that the detachment followed the orders of the accused which trickle down from him to the perpetrators. Be that as it may, their theory that the orders of the commands of the BH army were followed at all is simply untrue because all of the evidence suggests otherwise. Awad, in his evidence on compliance with orders: "Question: The command was issuing orders but unlike other units of you failed to comply with these orders. You simple made your own calls as to whether you would accept an order or not. Would this be a fair summary of what you said? Awad's answer was: "Yes." Hasanagic, the commander of the 35th Division, talked about compliance with the tasks assigned to the detachment. He said: "They were given assignments just as other units were. They, however, failed to perform those assignments as required. They preferred to carry out assignments as they saw fit." "Question: So whenever they decided not to be involved in an action that was their own call and no one had the power to issue any further orders to them about that. Am I right?" "Answer: Yes." Now, Your Honours, I wish to address the OTP's interpretation of the Hadzihasanovic appeals judgement and I will come to my next answer to your question. Talking about the OTP's interpretation or understanding of the appeals judgement, what they're trying to put to you is this: If at all possible, disregard it. Nevertheless, Your Honours, that is simply impossible. They are trying to tell that you the evidence in the Hadzihasanovic case is different from the evidence in this case, which is true. And how true, Your Honours, and how different. It is precisely the witnesses invoked by the OTP in order to prove the difference between this case and the Hadzihasanovic case. These are members of the detachment. These are insiders. These are members of the BH army, low-ranking one, foreign Mujahedin. That is what you are hearing from the OTP. But it is these witnesses that shed the most light on the issue of effective control over the Mujahedin in general and the El Mujahedin Detachment. As you have surely realised, Your Honours, I am not frequently invoking these members of the BH army where suggestions have been made that they should not be lent any credence. Precisely because of that, I think particularly illustrative were their star witnesses, insiders. We had to travel to Sarajevo twice because of them which is unprecedented in the history of this Tribunal. E-326, an interview by witness Hamad to the German magazine Der Spiegel. Hamad confirmed the authenticity of this interview. He stated: "There wasn't a single Bosnian general that had the power to order us anything." And this is the story of the meetings with General Alagic that you heard today, that was described for your benefit today and that Hamad talked about. That's all fine, meetings, talks, conversations, however, this is not about meetings, encounters and decisions that were taken; this is about proofing effective control. Do I have the power to order something to one of my subordinates and will my subordinates then comply with the order or not? That is what is at stake in this trial. Let's look at what Awad has to say: "Whenever we agreed to do something, an order like that would be formally issued to us. However, whenever there was no agreement, then no combat action or attack would be executed." This is from is from PW-9 on the 16th of November, 2007: "Therefore, would it be a fair conclusion that between the El Mujahedin Detachment and the commands of the army, the 35th Division OG North or indeed the 3rd Corps, there was rather cooperation, then subordination?" He answered: "That is correct. And I think I have already pointed this out a number of times." That is what PW-9 has to tell us. One thing that didn't happen in the Hadzihasanovic case happened here before this Trial Chamber. Even without such statements and such evidence, the Appeals Chamber found that the 3rd Corps commander had no effective control as regarded the counts of the indictment. You, Your Honours, are facing a situation where there is even far less evidence than in that case about the existence of effective control. You have seen evidence coming from a number of sources talking about control over the El Mujahedin Detachment. You saw textbook combat reports. PW-9 claims that these were being sent on a daily basis to the Islamic Cultural Centre in Milan throughout combat operations. These are E-1389 and E-1201. You, Your Honours, also had a chance to look at intercepted fax messages, including the one dated the 28th of November, 1993, Exhibit 127, addressed to the superiors of the El Mujahedin Detachment with addresses abroad. You have evidence before you that simply wasn't there in the Hadzihasanovic case, but it's here now and you have it in front of you. This evidence talks about the setting up of Mujahedin camps across Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Dzemat, the Shura, the sheikh Saban who was the one true authority for the detachment and his links with the Al Jama Al-Islamiyah. You have evidence on the independent financing of the detachment we explained all of this in our brief in paragraphs 972 through 1016 and that's why I'm not going back to that now. In paragraph 44 of the OTP's final brief, the OTP state that the indicators of effective control applied by the Trial Chamber in the Hadzihasanovic case showing effective control were recognised and accepted by the Appeals Chamber. However, Your Honours, that is only true to a very small extent. Much rather, it is hardly true at all. Quite the contrary, in fact. The Appeals Chamber found that the Trial Chamber had erred in assessing evidence in relation to indicators of effective control. Throughout much of this particular chapter of the appeals judgement some evidence was misjudged; other evidence was not taken into account at all. Be that as it may, we reply to your question number 8 on additional indicators taken into account by the Hadzihasanovic appeals judgement. This is also in evidence in this case.
