In keeping with your requirements, we drew up a table for ease of handling and so that you could better follow our reply to your question number 8. You should have it on the monitors in front of you, Your Honours, or at least I hope so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There is a table on my monitor. Thank you very much, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you can see, Your Honours, the table contains four columns. The first column shows the indicator from the appeals judgement. The second column shows the comment of the Appeals Chamber in the Hadzihasanovic trial. The third column shows additional criteria showing that there was no effective control over the Mujahedin. We marked that as pre-EMD or indeed the El Mujahedin Detachment. The fourth column shows the appropriate paragraphs of the Defence final brief or the appropriate exhibits, unless specified in our brief. Your Honours, my learned friend has just indicated to me that it might be a good idea to deal with the table after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you going to be long? You still have a minute to go? Would you rather take the break now?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a table that runs into a total of nine pages. We might as well start now, but we wouldn't be gaining any ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is one thing that perhaps we can do. We could perhaps distribute copies of this table, if the Chamber finds that helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Has it not been uploaded? We'd like it distributed. Thank you very much. Please do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, indeed. Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We'll take a break and come back at half past 12.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you for the hard copies, Madam Vidovic. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I will now be dealing with the table, specifically the first indicator reviewed by the Appeals Chamber in the Hadzihasanovic trial. In the middle column, we talk about additional criteria showing that there was no effective control over the El Mujahedin and the El Mujahedin Detachment. Evidence on that can be found in the paragraphs stated in column number 4. If there are not paragraphs from the brief, then we refer to specific exhibits. As far as the first indicator is concerned, contained in the Appeals judgement, what we are saying is this: Based on the evidence of Prosecution Witness Hogg, based on what he wrote in the article, the Mujahedin operated as gangs, and the Bosnian command wasn't able to control them. Secondly, the Mujahedin failed to heed the Bosnian authorities. Thirdly, the Mujahedin failed to follow any orders coming from officers of the BH army; rather, they followed orders from their own superiors. This is something that Hamad said. That is before the El Mujahid Detachment. During its existence, orders of the command of the BH army, on the resubordination of the El Mujahid Unit, were attempts to place this unit under control; however, the El Mujahedin Detachment did not follow any orders in relation to preparations for combat activity, or in those pertaining to movements to other areas. The El Mujahedin Detachment refused to follow any orders to do with their involvement in the fighting. The El Mujahedin Detachment refused to follow any orders in relation to joint actions with other units. They did not follow any orders in relation to the submission of reports to the commands of the BH army. They refused to allow the commander of the 35th Division and UNPROFOR members to pass through the Donja Blizna area. They were adamant that they should turn away and be sent back. The commander was not informed. The command of the El Mudjahedin Detachment did not submit any orders to the command of the BH army that had to do with the application of the Geneva Conventions. Delic's actions an order to do with the El Mujahedin Detachment fall far short of meeting the requirements for effectively control. That was the first indicator. The second indicator, as of course everything else that we talk about in your brief - and there is no need to repeat that now - the second indicator is how the units in question operated in battle prior to the establishment of the El Mujahedin Detachment. The Mujahedin were acting independently during the actual fighting. The relations between the Mujahedin and the BH army were not those reflecting subordination. Much rather, it was a relationship of cooperation. The Mujahedin were only involved in the fighting when the conditions that they themselves required were met. The Mujahedin were adamant that their commanders should exercise command in battles. The Mujahedin administration, including their military leaders, was submitting reports to al-Qaeda. Again, this is on Hamad's authority. There was a rift between the commands of the BH army, on the one hand, and the Mujahedin, on the other. The Mujahedin tried to kill the commander of the 7th Muslim Brigade -- one of the commanders of the 7th Muslim Brigade. Effendi Karalic. As for when the El Mujahid Detachment was established, it paid scant respect to the BH army, its flag, or its commanders. Members of the detachment did not wear BH army insignia, nor did they carry BH army ID in the fighting. In combat, the detachment was acting independently and was not working with the BH army. The relationship between the two was not a relationship of subordination, but rather one of cooperation. The leadership of the detachment took --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt, Madam Vidovic. Maybe if you just give us the indicators on the very left column, now that have you given us the paper, we can look through them. I realise that some of the things that you are reading are repeatedly. I mean, the Mujahedin acted independently, on page 2. You said that also on page 3. Maybe you could just give us the left ones.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in order for you to understand why there is repetition here, we review the situation as in the indictment, the situation prior to the establishment of the detachment, and then after the establishment of the detachment. That is why it is sometimes the case that an indicator is repeated. We're looking at the situation before the establishment. For example, the Mujahedin were involved in the fighting. Likewise, the El Mujahedin Detachment was operating independently while involved in the fighting, if my understanding is correct. So, hence, the repetition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may proceed. Okay. Proceed the way you are proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. The leadership of the El Mujahedin took the final decision on whether the detachment would engage in the fighting; therefore, the BH army could in no way rely on their involvement in the fighting. The El Mujahedin set the conditions for their involvement in the fighting. The El Mujahedin Detachment refused to be involved in the fighting. The El Mujahedin did not follow the order of the 35th Division on establishing a command post at a location where they were required to do so; rather, the El Mujahedin Detachment took their own decision on the location of the command post. The El Mujahedin did not follow orders in relation to the way an attack should proceed all the time when it should commence. The El Mujahedin Detachment did not pay any heed to the plans of the 35th Division. The El Mujahedin Detachment carried out independent reconnaissance and did not -- My apologies, Your Honour. The El Mujahedin Detachment carried out independent reconnaissance and did not submit any reconnaissance reports to the BH army commands. The members of the detachment taunted, threatened, and attacked BH army troops. The detachment did not comply with the security warnings issued by the BH army commands, which resulted in tragic consequences. The El Mujahid Detachment did not allow the 35th Division to take certain areas at the time when it should have been done, and this exposed the units to fire from Serb Montenegrin artillery which caused casualties. The detachment did not designate guides who would take the units to designated areas on time. The detachment seized the war booty from BH army, under threat of weapons, and took the booty to its camp. The detachment did not submit even the basic reports to the BH army commands about the personnel strength and the equipment and materiel at its disposal. The detachment did not submit military reports to what were purportedly its superior commands. The 35th Division never managed to establish contact with the detachment, in terms of security. The detachment never submitted any intelligence or security reports. The detachment did not submit any morale supports --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The detachment did not submit any reports as to the lines they had reached. And now we move on to the third indicator.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Can I just ask you for clarification. When you say that the El Mujahid Detachment did not submit military reports upwards in the system, do you mean to include both written reports and oral reports? So no reporting was made whatsoever, neither in writing nor orally. Is that your point?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I would like to say the following: The BH army does have rules of reporting. You have Exhibit 22. It is the decree on armed forces, and it quite clearly defines the relationship between various commands, the relationship of subordination within the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina; and it is stipulated that the subordinate must report to the superior, and so on, from the bottom to the top. So there is the obligation to report, in accordance with the rules that were put in place by the army. As regards your question about oral reporting, I would like to say the following. Of course, there can be oral reports, but in this case, in this specific case the Honourable Trial Chamber has to make a distinction between arrangements that are put in place, discussions, cooperation, and to define the relationship between two parties after fighting, whether this is cooperation or reporting. Of course, Your Honours, the two parties or the two units cooperating. Let's take a unit from the HVO and a unit from the BH army, this is what General Karavelic talked about in Krajina. Concerted action. Of course those units will keep each other informed about the lines that they reached in combat and about their casualties. This is cooperation, Your Honours. That's not reporting. But, of course, oral reports exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does Exhibit 22 prescribe written reports only or does it allow for oral reports?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, Exhibit 22 defines the rules on reporting. So it does not explicitly say whether it is written or oral reporting, but I would like to refer to some other exhibits here, Your Honour. You will recall, or, rather, I can't now recall the number off the top of my head, but now I'm talking about the documents that refer to the Kakanj command post and General Hadzihasanovic's order about how reports are to be submitted, and he orders the corps commanders to submit written reports. I will obtain this information and I will give you a specific reference as I go along. So now we have come to the third segment, presence of other authorities over the units in question. Your Honours, the Hadzihasanovic and Kubura judgement considered this issue of presence or absence of other authorities over the units in question before the El Mujahedin Detachment was set up -- Your Honours, before I move on to this, let me just go back and tell you that the document defining the way in which reporting is to be done is Exhibit 371, and it says the corps command and the unit commands must submit their reports to the Kakanj command post, and when you say "send," it means that they have to be in written form. This is the implication. So before the El Mujahid was established, the Mujahedin were under the control of external bodies, including the al-Qaeda, according to Ali Ahmad Ali Hamad. According to Ali Ahmad Ali Hamad, al-Qaeda organised the arrival of the Mujahedin to Bosnia and decided who would go there to fight and what unit they would join. The BH army did not appoint the leaders of the Mujahedin groups. The Mujahedin sent their reports abroad. According to witness Ali Hamad, they sent them to al-Qaeda. The El Mujahedin Detachment had its own goals, and its own political and military organisation. According to Hamad, the detachment had close links with international terrorist organisations, which inevitably includes al-Qaeda. The El Mujahedin Detachment military commanders, Muatez and Vahidin were members of al-Qaeda, according to Hamad, and they submitted their reports to al-Qaeda. Some El Mujahedin Detachment members were under the direct patronage of foreign intelligence services. The El Mujahedin Detachment had substantial links with some circles in the Republic of Croatia. The El Mujahedin Detachment was financed and supported by some Islamic organisations and by some Arab humanitarian organisations. The El Mujahedin Detachment received large sums of Monday directly or indirectly from officials from Qatar. The El Mujahedin Detachment secured funds for salaries and other monetary remunerations for its members abroad. The Islamic Cultural Centre in Milan and its director Sheik Anwar Saban were de facto authorities over the El Mujahedin Detachment. The El Mujahedin Detachment sent its reports about various problems to Saban. Abu Maali, the EMD commander respected and obeyed Saban who was the actual leader of the EMD. Saban had the power to issue fatwas that were binding for the El Mujahedin Detachment. The El Mujahedin Shura decided about the military organisation of the detachment, including its activities on the front line and elsewhere. The Shura was not responsible to anyone in the BH army, at any command level. The authority of the detachment military commanders stemmed from the powers vested in it by the Emir and the Shura. The Shura decided to set up the detachment and to disband it. The El Mujahedin Detachment enjoyed the support of some representatives, some figures from political and religious authorities in Bosnia and Herzegovina, high-ranking ones. It also enjoyed some support of local politicians from Zenica, Travnik, Zavidovici, and Tesanj. The commander of the 35th Division expected the Zavidovici municipality leadership to solve some problems that related to the EMD. The EMD enjoyed support from some Islamic clerics and had frequent contacts and support of the muftis from Zenica and Travnik, religious leaders, in other words. And this brings me to the fourth indicator, authority to apply disciplinary measures. Your Honours, before the El Mujahedin Detachment was set up, the BH army had no way to replace the Mujahedin commanders. Only the Mujahedin leadership had the ability to actually punish them. The Mujahedin had their own military court in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and al-Qaeda ordered its group to arrest its members. That's what we heard from Hamad. The BH army military police was unable to take any measures against the Mujahedin. The BH army was unable to file any criminal reports against the Mujahedin. The Mujahedin had their own disciplinary system and rules. The El Mujahedin, the information that pertained to the identity of the El Mujahedin Detachment members were not available to the army. The El Mujahedin Detachment did not allow access to its camps. The El Mujahedin Detachment refused to appoint a person who would mediate between the El Mujahedin Detachment and the BH army about security issues. The Shura dealt with all disciplinary issues and imposed disciplinary measures. It was impossible to carry out any inquiry or investigation when it would have to involve members of the El Mujahedin Detachment. The detachment had its own rules about prisoners of war. Even the 3rd Corps commander had to seek permission from the El Mujahid Detachment to be granted access to prisoners of war. The detachment command did not allow its members to be under the authority of the BH army. The Shura did not allow anyone outside of the El Mujahid Detachment to meddle in its affairs. The El Mujahedin Detachment took by force those of its members that had been arrested by the BH army -- the authorities of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. There is no evidence to indicate that any members of the El Mujahedin Detachment have ever been prosecuted by a military court of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the war. And, finally, Your Honours, we analysed the appeals judgement, the part of the appeal judgement that pertains to other relevant allegations outside of those that were discussed by the Trial Chamber in the Hadzihasanovic/Kubura case. Paragraph 212, before the El Mujahedin Detachment was set up, it was the ECMM who carried out an exchange of the Mujahedin fighters, not the BH army. This was admitted into evidence and tendered by the Defence. This is about Zivko Totic; Awad testified about that. We have paragraph 277 about the El Mujahedin. A member of the BH army arrested by the El Mujahid Detachment was not released been the BH army demanded his release. He was released only after the Travnik mufti, Avdibegovic, intervened. Paragraphs 228 and 230, before and after the establishment of the detachment, regarding the use of force, that's what we have said. It was impossible to use force against the detachment because they were scattered in various villages in Central Bosnia. They enjoyed support of the local population, and that is why to use force against them would mean to open up a third front line, which would, in turn, result in a blood bath. They had their own logistics and they were, in fact, stronger than the corps. This is what Prosecution Witness Awad said: Not only would the use of force be tantamount to conflict with the enemy forces, not forces under one's effective control, but it would also have widespread repercussions for army of Bosnia-Herzegovina itself. And this, Your Honours, brings me to the element of knowledge in Article 7(3) of the Statute. In the allegations of paragraph, 249, 250, and 251 of the Prosecutor's brief, concerning knowledge of the Mujahedin crimes, we provided a detail reply to this in paragraph 303 through 305 of our brief; and in other sections that concern the existence or non-existence of control over varios group, paragraph 265 through 345 of our brief. Your Honours, I'm now going deal with your question 7A. The question rests on the assumption that the accused had reason to know, or, indeed, knew back in 1995, that the El Mujahedin Detachment had committed serious violations of international humanitarian law. Then your question was: Would the fact that one continued to rely on the El Mujahedin's contribution to the war effort, without taking any monetary measures or disciplinary measures against its members, constitute the acceptance the risk that, indeed, this unit might commit further violations of international humanitarian law. Your Honours, the fact that you bore in mind when you posed this question, in actual fact, opens a number of substantial legal questions. First of all, in order to at all be relevant for review in this criminal case, the case against Rasim Delic, it would have to be appropriately pleaded in the indictment, in such a way that the details from which the responsibility of the accused would then stem are described as described and defined by the Chamber in its question. This, Your Honours, is a hard fact. If the indictment rests on this, this is something that should be pleaded in the indictment itself. There are many reasons for that. First of all, it concerns the relationship of subordination. Secondly, it concerns the question of necessary and appropriate measures. Thirdly, it concerns the question of the accused's knowledge under Article 7(3) of the Statute. The jurisprudence of this Tribunal deals with the importance of pleading in a number of rulings. Hard facts that an indictment is based on must be described. And, here, I invoke the jurisprudence in Kupreskic Appeals judgement, paragraphs 888 and 889; next, Furundzija, paragraph 147; next, Krnojelec, Brdjanin, Blaskic Appeals judgements; so on and so forth. All of this having to do with the Article 21 and Article 18 of the Statute in order to make sure that an accused can have a fair trial. I will be invoking the Articles of the Statute, Article 21(4)(b) of the Statute, and 18(4), and 21(4) of the Statute, as well as Rule 47. I'm talking about the Rules of Procedure. Your Honours, you're asking a question about something that wasn't defined in the indictment. It wasn't described in the indictment. If it had been, I would have run this case differently. I would have focussed on challenging such a fact. Needless to say, in our case, the Prosecutor simply failed to plead this fact. Be that as it may, Your Honours, even if they had this single factor reliance on the El Mujahedin's contribution to the war effort, it would still not have constituted a decisive factor, not in relation to the question of there being or not being a relationship of subordination between the accused and the perpetrators; in this case, the detachment. And this would have been manifested through the effective control exercised by the superior officer over his subordinates. The Trial Chamber in Hadzihasanovic case ruled this way and so did the Kubura Chamber. Paragraph 213, they ruled that reliance on a units contribution in the fighting is no argument securing support for the conclusion on the existence of effective control.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May I interrupt, Madam Vidovic. the issue here is not effective control. It is really the question whether -- it is reason to know, in brief. Now, if, obviously, reason to know is a factual inquiry, the question is: If you knew - and it is an assumption in the question - if you knew that crimes have been committed by a unit, does your continued use of that unit give you notice that or give you reason to know, and this is quite apart from effective control. And because you're saying it was not pleaded in the indictment, my question to you is: Is it not implied in the reason to know? Isn't that in the factual inquiry that has to be undertaken in addressing the "reason-to-know problem"? In other words, does it have to be pleaded?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Your Honour. I understand your question. It is position of the Defence that an issue like this had to be pleaded in the indictment because of effective control. That is our position, and now I am going to deal exactly with what you are asking, Your Honour. If I look at your question in the overall context of knowledge as defined by Article 7(3) of the Statute, and if we assume that General Delic was aware of violations of international humanitarian law, we're not talking about just any developments now. Let us start out with the assumption that he was aware of what had occurred in Maline on the 8 June 1993. Let's assume he continued to rely on the detachment. Would that constitute an assumption of risk, the risk of further violations? Let me answer this question. Absolutely not, Your Honours. The El Mujahedin Detachment had not even been established by the time this occurred on the 8th June 1993. The order is dated the 13th August. I'm sure you remember that. That is what the situation was. The OTP are doing their best to bundle all of the Mujahedin into the detachment, but let me leave that aside for the time being. Let me be specific in relation to the very gist of your question. There is that event. Let us try to leave aside all the additional factors even as they concerned the El Mujahedin Detachment. Between that event that occurred on the 8th of June 1993 and 1995, all the events described in the indictment, we're talking about July and September 1995, a period of about two years had elapsed between the two, Your Honours. There were no reports indicating any violations of international humanitarian law by members of the detachment between its establishment on the 13th of August, 1995 and these events. This is simply too long a period. Besides, the place is now different where the El Mujahedin Detachment was operating, different from the place where the Mujahedin were operating in June 1993. You will remember that, on the one hand, we have the Travnik; and here we have, on the other, the Zavidovici municipality area. I will now invoke paragraph 267 of the Hadzihasanovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, before do you that, can I just sorry to interrupt you. Can we forget the Maline incident for the time being. Let us assume he was aware of violations of war or of laws of war in July 1995 and used them in September 1995. Would you address the question now, given that time span and those two incidents. Same question, but we just moving from June 1993. He became aware of the violations in July 1995, and then uses them in September 1995. Still an assumption.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. Let me answer in the following way: The issue of knowledge, as, indeed, any other element of Article 7(3) of the Statute, must be assessed within the framework of each accused's actual situation. Given that, we would need to deal with the actual situation of the accused: What was he doing at the time? Did he know? Did he not know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Vidovic, this question is an assumption. The assumption is he knew. I'm not saying it a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, I understand. Again, I would like to tell you this, Your Honour. Assuming there are several months between the two points in time, we're looking at a period over which certain isolated occurred, our position is that this would not in itself constitute knowledge. At any rate, I think the question, the way it was phrased, is this: Each of the actual situations encountered by an accused must be assessed individually: Did he know? Did he not know? If so, again, this falls under a time-period that was earlier on, which in no way implies that the accused was consistently violating the provisions of international humanitarian law. Please allow me just to finish one thing that I was trying to say. Why is this our position of Rasim Delic's Defence. I am invoking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Vidovic, your conclusion is that the fact of knowing, in 1993, that crimes had been committed by the Mujahedin did not represent a risk, such that General Delic would have taken; that is, as regards future combat, that would have taken place in 1994, for example, or in this particular case, in July and September 1994 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, Your Honour. This is not just my conclusion. This is indicated by the jurisprudence of this Tribunal. This was the position last taken in paragraph 267 of the Hadzihasanovic Appeals judgement. The Appeals Chamber noted, while ruling on the issue of Kubura's knowledge, based on his earlier omissions to punish crimes by his subordinates, I quote: "Acts of robbery carried out by Kubura`s subordinates at Omnak [phoen] on the 9th of June, 1993, and in Vares on the 4th of November 1993, are about five months and about 40 kilometres apart." That is what led them to conclude, in paragraph 269, that his knowledge of past crimes and his omission to punish them in itself was not sufficient to constitute any real knowledge on the part of the accused in relation to events for which he stood indicted. In the Delic case, we have the following situation: This was an isolated occurrence in relation to some Mujahedin back in 1993 - and that was the gist of your question, Your Honour - in a different area, 57 kilometres away; the distance in time being equally great. The Hadzihasanovic ruling talks about five months and 40 kilometres; and, here, we have a situation where the events were two years apart, the geographical distance being 57 kilometres. Our position is this: Even if he had known about this fact that you cite, it still doesn't mean he would have taken the risk or accepted the risk that this unit might commit further violations. Now about the alleged history of the likelihood that this unit might commit crimes. We rely to this in paragraphs 484 to 515 in 1109, 1110, and 710 through 746 of our final brief. We provided detailed explanation, and, Your Honours, I will be dealing more with the issue of knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We provided a detailed explanation in relation to bulletins, their distribution, and the fact that in the absence of General Delic these were distributed to persons who stood in for him or represented him. I won't be repeating that. As regards the requirement that the accused had to know, and now I'm talking about the event on the 21st of July, 1995, the Prosecution is trying to prove that there was imputed knowledge and here the Prosecution relies on the information that on the 22nd of July, 1995, in the bulletin that was sent to Kakanj, it was stated that the El Mujahedin Detachment captured, only captured, nothing else, 50 prisoners. Be that as it may, in paragraphs 557 through 570, we explained in detail why this information was not at the disposal of General Delic because at that time he was participating in talks in Croatia, in Split, and he did not go to Kakanj before the 29th of July, 1995. Witness Berbic was quite determined when he said that bulletins did not wait for General Delic to arrive but were handed into Hadzihasanovic in his absence. On the 14th of September, 2007, Berbic makes the following comment on the statement he had given to an OTP investigator. "Do you recall having said that you submitted bulletins personally to the Chief of Staff, of course in situations when General Delic was absent?" And he says: "As far as I can recall, I said that in his absence I would hand over the bulletin to the Chief of Staff or the highest ranking officer within the administration." Yesterday you heard from the Prosecution, Your Honours, that Berbic's testimony is irrelevant in light of the bulletins that were submitted through Exhibit 377, because, at that time when the bulletins arrived, Berbic was not in Kakanj at all. But this is not true, Your Honours, because as a member of the military security service, Berbic was in Kakanj from 1994. It is quite strange to hear the Prosecution say that Berbic's testimony is irrelevant, when the Prosecution called Berbic to come here to testify about those documents, and Exhibit 377 was admitted into evidence through him. Again, they don't like the actual outcome of his testimony, and now they claim that it is irrelevant. It is in fact quite relevant, because Mr. Berbic, as a member of the military security service, worked in Kakanj from July 1994 onwards and he was the head of the Kakanj military security service, and he knew quite well how the military security service functioned and what the procedure was for the submission of those bulletins. The first report about the prisoners of war taken in July was submitted by the military security service of the 35th Division to the military security service of the 3rd Corps on the 22nd of July, 1995. That's Exhibit 553, Your Honours. The Prosecution, therefore, cannot rely on the fact that it is stated in Exhibit 364 that Delic had visited the 3rd Corps command on or around the 21st of July, and on the basis of that, they conclude that information was at his disposal. Your Honours, this document bears the date of the 21st of July, which means that on the 22nd of July, General Delic could not have been there, because there has been so much evidence to prove that both on the 22nd and on the 23rd of July, General Delic was in Split. Fortunately for him, he was attending the Split Conference which was quite a public affair. So he was not there, not until the end of July. This is something that you heard about. What the Prosecution wants you to do regarding the issue of knowledge of those events, is to assume that this information was available to Rasim Delic. That is not in accordance with the law, and this is not a view accepted in the Tribunal's jurisprudence. The same thing goes for the knowledge requirement in Operation Farz. They claim that Delic did have information at his disposal about the capture and crimes committed against the prisoners of war and civilians in September 1995. To prove that Rasim Delic did have access to the information about prisoners of war, the Prosecution relies on the fact listed in paragraphs 379, 380, and 381 of its final brief, where it is alleged that this information was widely known in the 3rd Corps although this has not been proven. They rely even on rumours that were never confirmed as to their accuracy and this is what witnesses from the 3rd Corps told us. The Prosecution tries to construct the whole story and then, it says, Rasim Delic himself admitted that he controlled -- that he exercised control over this action. This is based on a report by a journalist. Rasim Delic was in constant contact with the 3rd Corps from Malaysia, in particular on the 14th of September, and therefore, according to the Prosecution, he did have this information at his disposal because of those contacts. If a conclusion were to be drawn about General Delic's knowledge, on the basis of those facts as is required by Article 7(3) of the Statute, that would be a clear-cut error in law. In the Celebici case the Appeals Chamber found as follows. This is paragraph 239: "Finally, the relevant information only needs to have been provided or available to the superior, or, in the Trial Chamber's words, in the possession of. It is not required that he actually acquainted himself with the information ..." Your Honours, jurisprudence, in all cases, does not dictate that the accused must acquaint himself with something, except in a situation where he has at his disposal clear information about a serious and clear danger that a crime would be committed or that the perpetrators are about to commit a crime that is charged in the indictment. That is his obligation. It is not his obligation as the Prosecution puts it here and this is what this judgement and many other judgements made quite clear. So he didn't have to actually acquaint himself with the information. In the Appeals Chamber's view, an assessment of the mental element required by Article 7(3) of the Statute should be conducted in the specific circumstances of each case, taking into account the specific situation of the superior concerned at the time in question. Thus, as correctly held by the Trial Chamber, as the element of knowledge has to be proved in these type of cases, command responsibility is not a form of strict liability. A superior may only be held liable for the acts of his subordinates if it is shown that he knew or had reason to know about them. "The Appeals Chamber would not describe superior responsibility as a vicarious liability doctrine in so far as vicarious liability may suggest a form of strict imputed liability." So this is paragraph 239 of the appeals judgement in the Celebici case. The same view was taken in the Appeals Chamber judgement in Blaskic case, paragraph 62. Finally, it is clear from the Prosecution brief that it is trying to impose on the accused liability in accordance with the concept of the so-called strict liability. It is quite clear, particularly from paragraph 384 of its brief, where they describe how Jasarevic, the chief of the military security service administration, received E-669. It was the intercepted fax that speaks about the 60 prisoners, and then that Jasarevic was one of Delic's immediate subordinates with whom he was in direct contact and their conclusion is this. It is simply incredible. It would be impossible to believe that he failed to relay this kind of information to him. But, Your Honours it is not up to the Prosecution to say what is credible, probable or improbable but to prove that Delic was in the possession of this information, that it was available to him, and the Prosecution has failed to prove that, and I will tell you why. In this case, and General Delic is quite fortunate that this is the case, we have a protocol of the military security service administration of the BH army General Staff - that's Exhibit E-1306 - which clearly shows the movement of a document through the chain of command, when it was received, and where it was forwarded. The protocol of the -- or the log-book of the BH army General Staff military security service shows quite clearly where the documents were forwarded. That's E-669, dated the 16th September 1995, that the Prosecution is referring to. You can see that this was distributed or, rather, put in the Vranduk file; whereas, the E-709, dated 22nd October, 1995, was sent to the Ministry of Defence, and to the state security service of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. They were not sent or forwarded to General Delic. Mr. Mundis, yesterday, referred to evidence by witness Vuckovic who said, in his 92 ter statement, the highest level should receive a report about this, either on that day or the next day, so either on the 16th or on the 17th of September, 1995. But what the Prosecution has neglected to mention is that this witness, when asked a follow-up question about this document - so it wasn't me asking those questions, it was the Prosecution asking questions about this document - the witness was quite clear in his answer during the examination-in-chief on the 7th of November: "I decided, in fact, that a summary of this document should make part of the bulletin, in brackets, for the agreement. This means that the analyst who was to receive this document should come to me to get instructions. "Be that as it may, it is quite obvious that this report was not made part of the next bulletin because I crossed it out, probably after consulting Colonel Popovic, who was the chief of the counter-intelligence section, or perhaps even consulting General Jasarevic." This is what the witness said when the Prosecutor asked the follow-up question. The Prosecution always does this. They take a small segment of a witness's testimony, and then he uses -- they use this to paint the picture, not the whole of the testimony. But at any rate, this is the 16th and 17th of September, 1993 [as interpreted]. You will remember that, at the time when this information came to the military security service, General Delic was not in Sarajevo at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to apologise. I apparently misspoke. I misspoke. I said, when this information was received in 1993, and I'm actually talking about 1995, September 1995. 16th and 17th of September, 1995. At that time, Delic was not in Sarajevo, and both documents and Witness Dedovic confirmed that. You will recall that on the 16th - I think it was on the 16th or maybe on the 17th - he came back from Malaysia, and then he remained in Croatia and was busy with the negotiations in Croatia. After that, he dealt with the fighting in Bosnian Krajina. The most important thing here, in this whole issue related to the knowledge of the accused, you saw clear evidence that the highest-ranking people in the military security service administration usually ordered the information about the El Mujahedin Detachment to be kept within the military security service. You will recall the two documents, E-66 and E-784, where there were handwritten instructions: This information is not to go outside of the military security service. So this is the situation that General Delic faced; and in such a situation, it is not realistic to speak about the probability that the information may have been relayed or, as Mr. Mundis said to you yesterday, General Delic had this information at his disposal if the information was at the disposal of the military security service. The military security service had its chief. You heard testimony from Mr. Vuckovic that he was the one who decided what information to forward. So you saw documents that quite clearly say keep information about El Mujahedin Detachment within the military security service. So what kind of reality are we talking about? How could one even think that this might have been at the disposal of General Delic? And the Prosecution had those documents, in particular if you have a situation where General Delic is preoccupied by completely different matters. Again, Your Honours, it is quite obvious that the Prosecution is trying to impose this responsibility based on the concept of strict liability, and we can see that from paragraph 378, where there is this description, indicating that the information that pertained to the capture of prisoners of war was published in two publications of the BH army in October 1995. On the basis of this, the Prosecution is putting to us that General Delic had information at his disposal that led to his knowledge that the El Mujahid Detachment had subjected prisoners of war to cruel treatment and murder, on the basis of nothing more or nothing less on the basis of the fact that it is stated in those publications that the detachment had captured several VRS officers. Even if such information had been received in and of itself, it would have meant nothing in October 1995. So, throughout this trial, the Prosecution is claiming that it is tantamount that if the information was at the disposal of the accused, that this is tantamount to him know being this mistreatment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam Vidovic, please tell me the following: You are saying that General Delic knew or are you saying that he had reasons to know? So are you trying to contest both?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I categorically challenge the fact that he had reason to know. What I'm trying to explain is this: General Delic was away from Sarajevo. When the information came in, he was most certainly not in Sarajevo. He had no reason to know. This information was not available to him, as simple as that. Secondly, I tried to explain that information was kept within the military security service, the instructions being very specific: Do not forward. How, then, could he have possibly have known? I challenge both: Him having reason to know or him knowing. Now on to something that has to do with your question. According to the Prosecution, the accused has inquiry notice on a crime even if potentially he is in a position to access information indicating that a crime has been committed. According to them, being privy to information includes a subordinate being privy to information with no evidence that a subordinate really forwarded the information to the accused. This notion, the accused must have known, instead of should have known, the Prosecutor wants you to conclude must have known. This is a notion that was applied in the Yamashita case, but the situation was entirely different. In the Yamashita case, the crimes were widespread, extensive, both in terms of territory and in terms of time. That's why the conclusion was reached that the accused must have known. Nonetheless, this notion was changed in the -- in the USA versus von Leeb case, where instead of the requirement of strict responsibility, we see conscious neglect of duty applied to this high command. The Additional Protocol I of the Geneva Conventions refutes this standard, as well as the UN Commission For War Crimes. The same applies to all the judgements of this Tribunal so far. Therefore, the OTP can in no way require that you apply this standard. It is our position that the Prosecutor has failed to show knowledge under Article 7(3) of the Statute. Your Honours, I have very, very little left, a few words. As to necessary and reasonable measures to prevent or punish, we explained this in section 8, B, 5, and there is no reason for me to go back to that. I will just respond to your question 7b, because this is something that I omitted to do so far. Your question was: Would the request by the 3rd Corps to launch an investigation to a civilian and military prosecutor have met the requirement for the accused to have taken the necessary and appropriate measures to punish the perpetrators? Your Honour, again, I must invoke the Tribunal's jurisprudence, in terms of the accused performing his duty in terms of preventing or punishing. Each case must be assessed on an individual basis. The Appeals Chamber in Hadzihasanovic/Kubura case, paragraph 151, confirms: What constitutes reasonable and necessary measures is not a matter of law, it is a matter of proof. In that case, as in the Blaskic case, paragraph 72, the Trial Chamber found that a commander could still meet the requirement of punishing by informing appropriate authorities. Our position is well known. The request by the corps commander to -- a request by the corps commander to a civilian military prosecutor would have met that requirement. In the Hadzihasanovic case, the Trial Chamber found that the commander of the 3rd Corps met this requirement by filing a criminal report with the municipal public prosecutor in Bugojno. That's paragraph 154 of the Hadzihasanovic appeals judgement. Finally, Your Honours, I wish to conclude with another example from the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, as it concerns general principles established in relation to circumstantial evidence which the OTP base their case on. Hadzihasanovic Appeals judgement, paragraph 286. The Appeals Chamber notes that this standard is in keeping with the general principles established in the practice in relation to circumstantial evidence. More specifically, a case based on circumstantial evidence is made up of different kinds of evidence on different circumstances. Taken together, they point to the accused's guilt because, if combined, they could only exist because the accused actually committed the crimes that he stands indicted for. Such a conclusion must be established beyond a reasonable doubt. It is not sufficient that a mere reasonable conclusion be drawn from such evidence. This has to be the only reasonable conclusion available at all. The only reasonable conclusion available at all. As long as there is any other conclusion that is equally reasonable and available to the Trial Chamber, and that also happens to be consistent with an accused's innocence, this accused must then be acquitted. Thank you very much, Your Honours. My learned friend, Mr. Robson, will be addressing you with a remainder of our closing argument tomorrow. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The Chamber will adjourn until 9.00 tomorrow morning, same courtroom. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 11th day of June, 2008, at 9.00 a.m. 18 19 20 21 22 23 24
